theme: True repentance, the heart beneath the sacrifice
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 51. After the Day of Atonement, this psalm shows the heart that stands behind the sacrifice. Read it as a prayer you could pray yourself, and notice how David asks for what the sacrifices could not give.
settingTheScene: The title of the psalm says it is “A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” It is David’s prayer after his sin with Bathsheba and his murder of Uriah (2 Samuel 11 and 12). It is the greatest of the penitential psalms. The situation is particularly striking against the background of Leviticus. David’s sin was deliberate, and the sacrifices of Leviticus 4 covered only unintentional sin. He has no sacrifice to bring. All he can do is throw himself on God’s mercy.
observation: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions” (v. 1).
“Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin!” (v. 2).
“Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (v. 4).
“Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me” (v. 5).
“Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (v. 7).
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (v. 10).
“Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me” (v. 11).

“For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (vv. 16-17).
interpretation:
Psalm 51 is the honest prayer of someone who has sinned deeply and knows it. David uses the vocabulary of Leviticus: “wash,” “cleanse,” “purge with hyssop” (the plant used in the cleansing rituals of Leviticus 14). But he cannot use the sacrifices, because there was no sacrifice for what he did. He is thrown back entirely on God’s mercy. His first word is “mercy,” and the basis of his appeal is not his own repentance but God’s “steadfast love,” the same word you read in Exodus 34:6.

The famous line, “Against you, you only, have I sinned,” does not mean that David’s sin did not hurt Bathsheba or Uriah. It means that all sin is ultimately against God. The wrong to people is real, but the deepest wrong is to the one who made them in his image. A person who truly sees his sin sees that it is first of all an offense against God.

Notice that David says his problem goes deeper than his actions. “I was brought forth in iniquity.” He is not excusing himself. He is saying that sin is not just something he did. It is something he is. This is why he prays, “Create in me a clean heart.” He does not ask for help to do better. He asks for a new creation. The word “create” is the same one used in Genesis 1:1. Only God can make a clean heart, as only God can make the world.

The ending is the center of the psalm. “You will not delight in sacrifice… the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.” David is not rejecting the sacrificial system. In verse 19 he looks forward to right sacrifices being offered again. He is saying that sacrifices without a broken heart are empty. The system always depended on the heart of the worshiper, and God has always looked for it.

Psalm 51 is not a way to get around the Day of Atonement. It is the prayer of the person who knows what it means.
connection: Jesus told a parable of a tax collector who beat his chest and prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” and went home justified (Luke 18:13-14). Paul quotes Psalm 51:4 in Romans 3:4. The “clean heart” and “right spirit” echo God’s promise in Ezekiel 36:25-27. John says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). In Christ, the broken heart finds the sacrifice it needs.
application:
Make this psalm your own prayer today. Read it aloud slowly, and let it lead you to confess whatever is on your heart.

If you carry guilt over something you have already confessed, remember the promise that God does not despise a broken and contrite heart.

Ask God to create in you the clean heart you cannot make yourself.
prayerPrompts: Pray the words of Psalm 51 in your own words, telling God what you need cleansed.
Ask him to create a clean heart in you.
Thank him for Jesus, in whom your confession is answered.
